en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-mahākṣatradharmaparyāya*, also known as the *Sūtra on Consecrating Buddha Images*, translated by the Qin śramaṇa Shi Shengjian:
“Mahākṣatradharma, devas, humans, and elders, listen clearly! As for those who have attained human birth...”
It is difficult; so too is the unsurpassed Way.
Human life is difficult to obtain, and an encounter with a Buddha’s world is difficult to find.

When Śākyamuni Buddha was originally in the time of incalculable kalpas (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), while his body was still that of a layman (*avadāta-vastra*), he accumulated merit and virtue, constantly self-reproaching in every birth.
Transmigrating through the five realms of existence, he did not covet wealth or treasures but gave away his own body in charity.
He eventually became the crown prince of a king and was born on the eighth day of the fourth month at midnight, when the morning star appeared.
Upon touching the ground, he took seven steps and raised his right hand, saying:
"In the heavens above and on the earth below, I shall be the teacher for all people.
When the Prince was born, both heaven and earth shook violently.

The seventh Brahmā Heaven, Śakra, the second King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and the first Four Heavenly Kings all descended; they brought twelve kinds of fragrant bathing water and various flowers to bathe the Prince’s body.
"The Prince established himself as a Buddha and opened the way to perceive the Dharma, thereby instructing all people in the world.
The Buddha told the people of the world:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions were all born at midnight on the eighth day of the fourth month;..."
The Buddhas of the ten directions all leave their homes and enter the mountains to practice the Way at midnight on the eighth day of the fourth month;
the Buddhas of the ten directions all attain the Way of the Buddha at midnight on the eighth day of the fourth month;
the Buddhas of the ten directions all enter parinirvāṇa at midnight on the eighth day of the fourth month.
The Buddha said:
"Why is the eighth day of the fourth month used?

It is because at the junction of spring and summer, calamities and transgressions are all concluded; all things are universally born and no toxic vapors have yet circulated; it is neither cold nor hot, and the seasonal air is harmonious and appropriate."

Now, because it is the Buddha’s birthday, the people of the heavens and the world together contemplate the Buddha’s merit and bathe the Buddha’s image as if he were still present; for this reason, it is displayed to the people of the world.
The Buddha said:

"When I was a bodhisattva in the world, thirty-six times I became Śakra, the Heavenly King; thirty-six times I became a Golden Wheel-turning King; and thirty-six times I became a Universal Monarch who flies through the air."

Today, among you virtuous ones, whoever possesses a benevolent heart and good intentions, who remembers the grace and virtue of Śākyamuni Buddha, and who seeks the foremost merit by bathing the image of the Buddha with incense and flowers—this shall be witnessed and known by the devas and spirits.
The Buddha said:
"A human body is difficult to obtain, and the Buddha’s sutras are difficult to hear.
One who can practice self-restraint and offer even the wealth of a common household to bathe the image of the Buddha will have their aspirations fulfilled."
If one desires to seek the unconditioned path that transcends the world and never again wishes to encounter birth and death, it can be attained;
if one desires to seek diligent and courageous progress, establishing oneself like Śākyamuni Buddha, it can be attained;
if one desires to seek the flight-like instruction of Mañjuśrī and the non-regressing bodhisattvas, and to possess the complete marks of a person, it can be attained.
If one seeks to become a pratyekabuddha or an arhat, it can be attained;
if one seeks to close off the three evil realms and be reborn fundamentally in the heavens or the human world, it can be attained;
if one seeks to become the seventh Brahmā or Śakra, the king of the second Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, it can be attained.
If one wishes to become a flying emperor, it can be attained;
if one wishes to be wealthy and noble within the world, it can be attained;
if one seeks to be born into a family with wealth in the hundreds of millions, it can be attained.
If one desires a hundred sons and a thousand grandsons, it can be obtained;
if one desires long life and freedom from illness, it can be obtained.

People of the world would rather lose a piece of flesh from their own bodies than lose a single coin. Yet, in life one does not bring a single coin with one, and at death one does not take a single coin away; wealth and possessions remain behind in the world, and thus, upon death, one must undergo suffering and affliction.
"By using this to bathe the Buddha, one shall be accompanied through birth and death without interruption.

The Buddha said, "The various devas, Brahmās, Śakras, ghosts, spirits, and nāgas within and without Jambudvīpa shall all protect those who bathe the image of the Buddha; by virtue of these causes and conditions, they shall attain the path of the Buddha’s Nirvāṇa."
The Buddha said:
"Those who offer fine incense and bath water to bathe the images of the Buddha will themselves obtain blessings; wherever they go, they will be pure and their fame will spread.
Those who offer fine flowers to the Buddha will themselves obtain blessings; they will be handsome and their complexion will be peerless."
"Those who offer silk banners to the Buddha shall obtain blessings for themselves; wherever they are born, they will always naturally receive excellent clothing without end.

The Buddha said, "I attained the state of Buddhahood only after accumulating merit over many lifetimes, practicing virtue with utmost sincerity, and cultivating the perfections of morality, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom."
"Whatever one obtains from making offerings to the image of the Buddha should be divided into three parts:
the first for the money of the Buddha, the second for the money of the Dharma, and the third for the money of the Bhikṣu Saṃgha."
Buddha-money is used to fashion images of the Buddha, whether of gold, copper, wood, clay, plaster, or paint, and with this Buddha-money they are restored and maintained.
Dharma-money is used for constructing multi-storied towers, stupas, monasteries, fences, walls, and inner and outer buildings; this is Dharma-money.
If the Bhikṣu Saṃgha possesses ten thousand coins, one thousand bhikṣus shall divide them among themselves.
If there are no monks present, one should perform only one part [of the ritual]; however, one part must be given as a legal fee (*dharmika-mūlya*).
Even when dividing among several people, it should be divided into three parts, and one part should be set aside for distribution.

Regarding funds held for future purposes or the Sangha’s property, not even a single coin above that amount may be used frivolously. If one privately takes even a single coin for private use or for acts of charity, one will experience extreme poverty in this life and suffer long-term consequences hereafter.
It would be better to cut one's own flesh with a sharp blade to give as alms to others than to offer a single coin to the Buddha while privately claiming it as a personal favor;
it would be better to swallow molten copper than to offer a single coin to the Buddha while treating it as a private act of kindness;

it would be better to throw oneself into a great fire than to offer a single coin to the Buddha for the sake of one's wife and children, or to provide them with cooked food together, for in this present life one shall suffer terror, and in future lives the soul shall undergo such agony.

Many people in the world conceive the intention to seek their desires; on the day they practice giving, they do not calculate whether it is little or much, but strive only to ensure their undertakings are abundant, until those who are respectful become utterly exhausted.
"The remains of the various dishes from the assembly have not been fully consumed;
what should be done with them? The Buddha said, "Whether it be little or much, they should all be sent to provide for the Dharma-upholding śramaṇas residing within Song Mountain Monastery."
If the community of monks divides the goods among themselves, they should expect to generate merit from the items thus distributed.
How could merit arise from eating what was sown in spring?
One should not divide the property among themselves and then give their shares to wives and children.
This is like planting seeds upon a stone; the roots and stems will be scorched away, and there will never be a time of growth.
Now, by taking the remaining merit of one's almsgiving and giving it again to the Sangha, this is called "giving once and receiving ten thousandfold."

"On the eighth day of the fourth month is the Buddha-bathing ceremony. One blends the three types of herbal incense—duliang, huoxiang, and aina—and kneads them together before soaking them in water; this constitutes the blue-colored water.
If the incense is insufficient, one may temporarily substitute it with indigo-black pigment and *qinpi*."
Take saffron and knead it with the hands before soaking it in water; by kneading it, one produces "red water.
If the saffron is insufficient or lacking, one may temporarily substitute it with facial rouge.
One should pound *kūṭaja* incense and then soak it to produce white water;
if the incense is scarce, one may supplement it with *hupen* (calamine powder), and if that is lacking, one may temporarily substitute it with white powder.
Pound the white arisaema and then soak it to produce yellow water;
if white arisaema is lacking, one may temporarily substitute with gardenia.
The "Dark Water" (xuánshuǐ) is black in color; it is the last [of the five] and is pure and clear. What we now see as well-water from the morning dew is merely called "Dark Water.
The above-mentioned five-colored waters for consecration are as detailed in the preceding memorial.

"Having completed the ritual of pouring pure water over the image, one wipes it with white silk or white cotton; after this, one performs a divination and pours water again, which is called the 'Ritual of Pure Pouring' (śuddhābhiṣeka)."
"The merit of this is no different from that of the foremost merit.

This *Mahāsthāmaprāpta-sūtra* (translated by Dharmakṣema) is recorded in the Song edition of the Tripiṭaka as the *Guanxi foxingxiang jing* (Sūtra on Bathing the Image of the Buddha), translated by Faju.
Upon examining the scriptural text, it was found to be conflated with the *Mahāsthavira-sūtra* (摩訶剎頭經) in the Song Edition of the Tripiṭaka; thus, the Song Edition is erroneous.

Now, according to the Derge edition, this sūtra is in fact the *Mahāsthavira-sūtra*, translated by Sengjian (聖堅). Following the Derge edition, I have accordingly changed the title of the sūtra and the name of the translator.
